quick: Regimen-specific IV, e.g. 20 mg/m2/day x5 or 75-100 mg/m2 q3-4 wk
Contraindicated (Category D); can cause fetal harm
Do not breastfeed; excreted in milk
Use with caution; not primarily hepatically cleared
Renal function, electrolytes, audiometry, CBC, neuro exam
summary: Cisplatin is a platinum-based cytotoxic used (usually in combination) for testicular, ovarian and bladder cancers and many other solid tumors. It is given by slow IV infusion with vigorous hydration, never by rapid IV injection or via aluminum-containing sets. A boxed warning highlights severe cumulative nephrotoxicity, plus myelosuppression, severe nausea/vomiting, ototoxicity (especially in children) and anaphylactic-like reactions.
indications: Metastatic testicular tumors (combination therapy after surgery/radiotherapy)
Metastatic ovarian tumors (combination with cyclophosphamide; or as single agent secondary therapy)
Advanced bladder cancer (single agent for transitional cell carcinoma no longer amenable to surgery/radiotherapy)
Other solid tumors per established regimens (e.g., head and neck, lung, cervical) as supported by oncology practice

dosage.d: 20 mg/m2 IV daily for 5 days per cycle
dosage.n: With other agents; slow IV infusion only
Do not give more often than every 3-4 weeks
Reduce to 50 mg/m2 q4 wk in heavily pretreated patients

admin: Administer only by slow IV infusion - NEVER by rapid IV injection
Do not use needles or IV sets containing aluminum (aluminum reacts with cisplatin, forming precipitate and loss of potency)
Pre- and post-hydrate vigorously to maintain urine output and reduce nephrotoxicity; consider mannitol/forced diuresis per protocol
Give antiemetic prophylaxis (cisplatin is highly emetogenic)
Verify renal function and electrolytes have recovered before each course; do not repeat more often than every 3-4 weeks
moa: Cisplatin enters cells and undergoes aquation; the reactive platinum species binds covalently to DNA, forming intrastrand and interstrand cross-links (predominantly at adjacent guanine N7 positions). These cross-links distort the DNA helix, inhibit replication and transcription, and trigger apoptosis. Its action is cell-cycle nonspecific, behaving like a bifunctional alkylating agent.

absolute: History of allergic reaction to cisplatin or other platinum-containing compounds
relative: Concurrent nephrotoxic or ototoxic agents (e.g., aminoglycosides)

preg: Pregnancy Category D - cisplatin can cause fetal harm and is contraindicated in pregnancy. Advise females of reproductive potential of the potential hazard and to avoid pregnancy; effective contraception is required during therapy.
lact: Cisplatin is excreted in human milk; patients receiving cisplatin should not breastfeed.
renal: Contraindicated in pre-existing renal impairment. Cumulative, dose-related nephrotoxicity is the major dose-limiting toxicity; ensure adequate hydration and confirm renal recovery before each course. It is potentiated by aminoglycosides.
hepatic: Cisplatin is not primarily cleared hepatically; specific hepatic dose adjustments are not defined, but use with caution and monitor, as hepatotoxicity can occur particularly at high doses/overdose.

major: Aminoglycoside antibiotics - potentiate cumulative nephrotoxicity (and additive ototoxicity); avoid
Other nephrotoxic or ototoxic drugs (loop diuretics, amphotericin) - additive renal/ear toxicity
Nephrotoxic contrast and NSAIDs - increased renal injury risk
moderate: Anticonvulsants (phenytoin) - plasma levels may become subtherapeutic; monitor and adjust
Live vaccines - avoid in immunosuppressed patients
Other myelosuppressive chemotherapy/radiation - additive marrow suppression
minor: Pyridoxine with altretamine - reduced response duration in ovarian cancer (avoid that combination)
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; additive nausea/vomiting and general toxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: Raises BUN/creatinine and uric acid; lowers Mg, K, Ca, Na; causes anemia/leukopenia/thrombocytopenia; may affect audiometry.

serious: Acute renal failure / cumulative renal insufficiency
Ototoxicity progressing to deafness (more pronounced in children)
rare: Cardiac abnormalities, vascular events (MI, stroke, thrombotic microangiopathy)

monitoring: Serum creatinine, BUN and creatinine clearance before and before each course; confirm recovery
Serum magnesium, potassium, calcium and sodium before each course and as needed
Complete blood counts (weekly) for myelosuppression nadir
Audiometry at baseline and periodically; neurologic exam for neuropathy
Liver function and signs of allergic reaction during infusion
counsel: Expect possible nausea/vomiting; take antiemetics as prescribed and report if uncontrolled
Drink fluids as advised - good hydration protects the kidneys
Report reduced urination, ringing in the ears or hearing changes, numbness/tingling, or signs of infection (fever)
Avoid pregnancy and breastfeeding; use effective contraception during treatment
Report any rash, facial swelling or breathing difficulty during/after infusion immediately
pk: Cytotoxic DNA binding within hours of infusion
Initial ~25-50 min; terminal (protein-bound platinum) several days
Platinum detectable in tissues for months; dosed every 3-4 weeks
Store at 20-25 C; do not refrigerate; protect from light
pearls: Boxed warning: severe cumulative nephrotoxicity, plus myelosuppression, severe nausea/vomiting, ototoxicity (worse in children) and anaphylactic-like reactions
Vigorous hydration (and sometimes mannitol-forced diuresis) is essential to limit kidney injury
Never give by rapid IV push and never use aluminum-containing needles/sets (precipitation and loss of potency)
Highly emetogenic - give triple antiemetic prophylaxis; hemodialysis does not remove protein-bound platinum
missed: Cisplatin is given as scheduled cycles in a supervised oncology setting, so there is no patient-managed missed dose. If a cycle/appointment is missed, contact the oncology team to reschedule; do not attempt to make up doses independently.
overdose: Acute overdose may cause renal failure, hepatic failure, deafness, ocular toxicity (including retinal detachment), severe myelosuppression, intractable nausea/vomiting and neuritis; death can occur. There is no proven antidote, and hemodialysis is largely ineffective because of rapid, high protein binding. Provide intensive supportive care and monitoring.
